source.title_on_document: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews

supplement.where: Appendices A-I on PDF pp. 16-46, cited in the main text as 'Supp. Table' and 'Supp. Figure'. The paper mentions no external supplement.
supplement.holds: The numerical tables behind the main-text figures: Tables 5-6 (validation, p. 20), Tables 7-8 (main alpha estimates, p. 21), Tables 23-27 (correlates, pp. 35-36; Table 26 gives alpha and CI (±) for the homogenization effect), and Table 31 (Nature portfolio data, p. 42). Also robustness tables (adverbs, verbs, nouns, document level, GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Claude 2.1), prompts (App. E), LLM settings (App. F), dataset details (App. G), and a sample-size theorem (App. I, pp. 45-46).

paper_design_summary: The authors estimate the share (alpha) of sentences substantially modified or generated by an LLM, using historical human reviews and GPT-4-generated reviews as reference corpora and validating the estimator on mixtures with known AI shares. They analyze public conference and Nature portfolio peer reviews across periods and, for post-ChatGPT conference reviews, compute each review's proximity to the centroid of its paper's review embeddings and compare estimated AI shares between the most convergent and most divergent review corpora (pp. 6-9, Secs. 4.1-4.7). This is an observational comparison of similarity across reviewers' outputs; no people were assigned to AI and no human creativity ratings were collected.

studies.label: Corpus analysis of ML-conference and Nature portfolio peer reviews before and after ChatGPT, with a homogenization comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing. The paper estimates the share of AI-modified sentences in existing public review corpora and compares it across years (before vs after ChatGPT's release on November 30, 2022) and across subsets of post-ChatGPT reviews.
assignment.quote: We collect review data for all major ML conferences available on OpenReview, including ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, and EMNLP, as detailed in Table 1.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Sec. 4.1 and Table 1; p. 42, Ethics Considerations (public, anonymous OpenReview data)

arms.name: Pre-ChatGPT reviews
arms.description: Official reviews written before ChatGPT's release on November 30, 2022: ICLR 2018-2023, NeurIPS 2017-2022, CoRL 2021-2022 (p. 6, Table 1), and Nature portfolio 2019-2022 (p. 42, Table 31). Used to train and validate the estimator and as the pre-period of the temporal trends (p. 21, Tables 7-8). Counts are reviews (e.g., ICLR 2023: 18,564), not people.

arms.name: Post-ChatGPT reviews
arms.description: Official reviews written after ChatGPT's release: ICLR 2024 (27,992 reviews), NeurIPS 2023 (14,389), CoRL 2023 (759), EMNLP 2023 (6,419) (p. 6, Table 1), and Nature portfolio 2022-2023 (6,200 reviews of 2,189 papers; p. 42, Table 31). AI was available; individual use is not observed and is estimated only at the corpus level.

participants.exclusions: No participants were recruited; the units are public reviews split into sentences. Only sentences with 2 or more words are used, and blank review sections add no sentences (p. 42, App. G). Technical keywords self-reported by authors on OpenReview are removed from the vocabulary (p. 4, Sec. 3.1). The number of distinct reviewers is not stated.
participants.who: Anonymous peer reviewers of ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, and EMNLP submissions (via OpenReview) and of papers in 15 Nature portfolio journals. The paper calls them human experts (p. 2) and counts reviews and papers, never reviewers.
participants.quote: In our work, we accessed this publicly available, anonymous peer review data through the public OpenReview API and confirm that we have complied with their terms of use.
participants.locator: p. 42, Ethics Considerations; review counts at p. 6, Table 1 and p. 42, App. G and Table 31

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT is the tool the paper studies, but reviewers' actual tools are not observed. The AI reference corpus was generated with GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, the June 13, 2023 snapshot; p. 42, App. F). Robustness checks train on GPT-3.5 (pp. 37-39, App. D.13), LLaMA-2 Chat (70B), and Claude 2.1 (p. 44, App. H). The homogenization analysis uses OpenAI text embeddings (p. 9).
ai_tool.how_used: Not observed per reviewer. The authors prompt GPT-4 with paper text to generate AI-written reviews that form the reference distribution Q for the estimator (p. 4, Sec. 3.4; p. 40, Figure 27). They report that the estimates are consistent with reviewers using an LLM to expand an outline or substantially modify their own review text (p. 8, Sec. 4.6; p. 10).

task.description: Writing peer reviews of submissions to ML conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL, EMNLP) and of papers in 15 Nature portfolio journals.

outcomes.name: Estimated share of AI-modified sentences (alpha) in each paper's most convergent review vs its most divergent review (the 'homogenization effect')
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each paper, the authors embed all its reviews with OpenAI text embeddings and compute the centroid. The review closest to the centroid is labeled convergent ('Homogeneous Reviews' in Table 26, 'Most Convergent Review' in Figure 10) and the farthest divergent ('Heterogeneous Reviews', 'Most Divergent Review'). They then estimate alpha (MLE share of sentences substantially modified by an LLM, adjective vocabulary) separately on the convergent corpus and on the divergent corpus. Similarity defines the groups and alpha is the compared quantity, so the result is an association between estimated AI use and similarity across reviewers of the same paper.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Most convergent review of each paper ('Homogeneous Reviews'), post-ChatGPT venues ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023, EMNLP 2023
contrasts.control_arm: Most divergent review of each paper ('Heterogeneous Reviews'), same venues
contrasts.reported: Table 26, alpha (CI ±), Heterogeneous Reviews vs Homogeneous Reviews: ICLR2024 7.2% (0.4%) vs 13.1% (0.4%); NeurIPS2023 6.1% (0.4%) vs 11.6% (0.5%); CoRL2023 5.1% (1.5%) vs 7.6% (1.4%); EMNLP2023 12.8% (0.8%) vs 19.6% (0.8%). Direction refers to the estimated AI share, which is higher in the convergent group; no test of the difference is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Sec. 4.7 'Homogenization Effect' and Figure 10; p. 35, Table 26

diversity_detail.metric: Each review's embedding distance to the centroid of the embeddings of all reviews of the same paper; the closest review is labeled convergent and the farthest divergent. The reported statistic is the estimated alpha in each group, not a similarity score.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI text embeddings ('OpenAI’s text-embeddings'); model version not stated
diversity_detail.computed_over: Within each paper, each review against the centroid (average embedding) of that paper's reviews; one convergent and one divergent review kept per paper.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: CI (±) reported per group in Table 26. Section 4.4 states that error bars for the main estimates are 95% confidence intervals over 30,000 bootstrap samples (p. 7); the paper does not restate the method for Table 26. No test of the difference between the groups is reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Sign: the paper reports AI share by similarity group, the reverse of similarity by AI use. A higher alpha among convergent reviews means estimated AI use goes with less diversity across reviewers (sign reversed relative to the codebook's diversity direction). The number of papers or reviews in each group is not stated. Nature portfolio reviews are not in this analysis. Box 1 labels it a 'Homogenization Correlation' (p. 3); the design is not causal.

company_involvement.description: Zachary Izzo (second author, marked equal contribution) lists the Machine Learning Department, NEC Labs America, an industry research lab. Acknowledged funding is from NSF, the Chan-Zuckerberg Initiative, and Stanford HAI. OpenAI models (GPT-4, text embeddings) are used as research tools.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations footnote; p. 11, Acknowledgments; p. 42, App. F; p. 9, Sec. 4.7

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: the authors collect existing public peer reviews and estimate AI use at the corpus level; no reviewers are randomly assigned to AI assistance (p. 6, Sec. 4.1; p. 42, App. G and Ethics Considerations). Criterion 2 is unclear: the reported counts are reviews and papers, and the number of distinct people whose reviews were analyzed is not stated (p. 6, Table 1; p. 42, App. G and Table 31); people counts remain null. Criterion 3 is met for the homogenization analysis: convergence/divergence is computed from each review's embedding proximity to the centroid of all review embeddings for the same paper, including the focal review (p. 9, Sec. 4.7 and Figure 10). Under codebook Secs. 1 and 3, writing compared across writers for similarity qualifies as output-scored diversity. Table 26 (p. 35) reports estimated AI shares for the similarity-defined groups, not similarity means or an effect of assigned AI assistance; this limits the result to observational context but does not negate the output-based similarity assessment. Core eligibility is no regardless of the unstated reviewer count because random assignment of AI is absent.

one_line_finding: The estimated share of review sentences substantially modified by an LLM was 10.6% at ICLR 2024 (1.6% at ICLR 2023), 9.1% at NeurIPS 2023, 6.5% at CoRL 2023, and 16.9% at EMNLP 2023, with no significant rise in Nature portfolio reviews (p. 21, Tables 7-8), and each paper's most convergent review had a higher estimated share than its most divergent review (ICLR 2024: 13.1% vs 7.2%; p. 35, Table 26).
open_questions: How many distinct reviewers contributed to the analyzed corpus, especially the convergent/divergent review groups? The PDF reports reviews and papers only (p. 6, Table 1; p. 42, App. G and Table 31). An author-confirmed count of unique reviewers would settle criterion 2; it would not change the core exclusion for absent random assignment.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they bear on none of the three questions (they measure AI-text prevalence, not creativity or diversity): alpha by year (p. 21, Tables 7-8; robustness Tables 12, 14, 16, 18, 30), by ICLR 2024 primary area (p. 24, Table 10), and by deadline, references ('et al.'), reply count, and reviewer confidence (pp. 8-10, Figures 7-9 and 11; pp. 35-36, Tables 23-25 and 27). Validation and robustness tables (Tables 5-6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21-22, 28-29, 32-33) test the estimator on semi-synthetic mixtures. Post-ChatGPT alpha: ICLR 2024 10.6%, NeurIPS 2023 9.1%, CoRL 2023 6.5%, EMNLP 2023 16.9%; Nature portfolio 2023 1.6% (p. 21, Tables 7-8). The data_url is the OpenReview API documentation the paper cites as its access route for the ML-conference reviews (p. 42, App. G); the paper gives no separate dataset URL, and Nature portfolio reviews were collected with a custom web scraper. The reconciler added source.supplement, which both raw forms omitted. Screener A's statement that the markdown stops at PDF page 21 is wrong: the markdown covers all 46 pages. Finalization: read the entire markdown conversion, including Appendices A-I, and checked the eligibility passages, reported estimates, confidence-interval entries, and corpus counts against the PDF text. No c011 challenge files were present; challenge_resolution is empty and n_corrected, n_rejected, and n_open count challenge dispositions only. The reconciled source.supplement already meets the current spec and is retained. This is an original observational corpus study, not a reanalysis of a randomized experiment; no post-exclusion people count is available to relabel as randomized. The finalizer resolves the former outcome/scope questions using codebook Secs. 1 and 3 and changes criterion 3 from unclear to met: 'Among the assigned reviews, the one with its embedding closest to the centroid is labeled as convergent, and the one farthest as divergent.' (p. 9, Sec. 4.7). This computed comparison across reviewers' writing meets the output-scoring requirement even though the displayed statistic is alpha by similarity group. It does not establish that AI caused homogenization or supply a similarity effect size. The two resolved questions are retained as resolved entries in final.open_items with nothing_needed and no remaining eligibility uncertainty; the missing unique-reviewer count remains open for criterion 2. The company description now states the documented affiliation and funding without the unsupported categorical assertion that no AI vendor is involved (p. 1, affiliations; p. 11, Acknowledgments). The data note states that no separate dataset URL is given, rather than claiming that no dataset is posted. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical reconciliation record; the final eligibility decision supersedes its earlier criterion-3 assessment.

open_items.item: Resolved former question: whether the homogenization analysis counts as observational diversity context. This concerned criterion 3, now met: review-to-centroid proximity classifies the outputs as convergent or divergent (p. 9, Sec. 4.7 and Figure 10). The comparison of alpha across these groups (p. 35, Table 26) remains a diversity-related observational association. Codebook Secs. 1 and 3 require output-based scoring and do not require similarity to be the dependent variable. No eligibility uncertainty remains from this question.

Resolved former question: whether peer-review writing is within scope. This concerned the task boundary for criterion 3. Codebook Sec. 1 explicitly includes writing whose outputs are compared across writers for similarity; this paper compares different reviewers' texts on the same submission (p. 9, Sec. 4.7). The task therefore qualifies for observational across_people context, and no eligibility uncertainty remains from this question.

Unstated number of distinct reviewers in the analyzed corpus and homogenization groups: an author-confirmed count of unique people whose reviews were analyzed would settle criterion 2. The PDF gives review and paper counts only (p. 6, Table 1; p. 42, App. G and Table 31). This cannot reverse core exclusion because criterion 1 is not met.
